title: Hash functions
syllabusUnit: Unit IV: Cryptographic Hash Functions & Hash Algorithms
covers: Properties, avalanche, birthday paradox, SHA family, collisions
learningGoals: You will be able to state the three core properties of cryptographic hash functions.
You will be able to demonstrate the Avalanche Effect with a 1-bit input flip.
You will be able to explain why the Birthday Paradox requires 256-bit digests.

lessonCards.title: The Digital Fingerprint
lessonCards.analogy: A blender that takes an entire encyclopedia or a single word and produces an exact 64-character smoothie.
lessonCards.coreConcept: A cryptographic hash function H(M) maps variable-length input to a fixed-length digest. It is strictly one-way (irreversible).
lessonCards.example: SHA-256 turns any data into exactly 256 bits (64 hex characters).

lessonCards.title: The Three Sacred Properties
lessonCards.analogy: 1. Impossible to reverse. 2. Impossible to find another text matching a target. 3. Impossible to find ANY two matching texts.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Pre-image resistance (one-way). Second pre-image resistance (given M1, cannot find M2 such that H(M1)=H(M2)). Collision resistance (cannot find any pair M1 != M2 with H(M1)=H(M2)).
lessonCards.example: Breaking collision resistance breaks digital signatures.

lessonCards.title: The Avalanche Effect & Birthday Attack
lessonCards.analogy: Dropping one pebble starts an avalanche that changes 50% of the mountain.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Flipping a single bit in the input changes ~50% of all output digest bits unpredictably. Due to the Birthday Paradox, finding a collision in an n-bit hash takes only 2^(n/2) operations.
lessonCards.example: An 80-bit hash can be cracked in 2^40 operations; a 256-bit hash requires 2^128 operations (safe).

questions.prompt: What is 'Pre-Image Resistance' in a cryptographic hash function?
options: Given a hash digest h, it is computationally infeasible to find any original message m such that H(m) = h
The hash function produces outputs of variable length
The hash function can be decrypted with a password
The hash function deletes duplicate files
questions.explanation: Pre-image resistance guarantees that the hash function is a one-way street: you cannot reverse the digest back to the input.
wrongExplanations: Correct! One-way property: infeasible to calculate input from output.
Hash digests are always fixed length.
Hashes have no keys and cannot be decrypted.
Hashes do not delete files.
questions.realWorldExample: Password storage relies on pre-image resistance so leaked database hashes cannot be easily inverted.

questions.prompt: In a cryptographic hash function, what does the 'Avalanche Effect' mean?
options: A 1-bit change in the input flips approximately 50% of the output digest bits
The computer processor speeds up over time
Hash digests get longer as files get larger
Files are deleted like falling snow
questions.explanation: A strong hash function ensures that even the tiniest change cascades through compression rounds, totally scrambling the output.
wrongExplanations: Correct! High diffusion causes ~50% of bits to invert unpredictably.
CPU clocks remain constant.
Digest length is strictly fixed (e.g. 256 bits).
Files are unaffected.
questions.realWorldExample: Hashing 'hello' vs 'Hello' in SHA-256 produces completely unrecognizable hex strings.

questions.prompt: Why does the 'Birthday Paradox' reduce the security of an n-bit hash function from 2^n to 2^(n/2) against collisions?
options: In a group of only 23 people, there is a 50% probability two people share a birthday; comparing pairs requires far fewer trials
Because computers crash on birthdays
Birthdays are always even numbers
Because calendar months have 30 days
questions.explanation: Finding ANY collision between two random inputs compares pairs (n choose 2), reaching a 50% chance of a match in only O(sqrt(N)) = 2^(n/2) steps.
wrongExplanations: Correct! The birthday bound means finding ANY collision requires only 2^(n/2) operations.
Hardware stability is unrelated.
Calendar dates are arbitrary.
Months do not dictate mathematical probability.
questions.realWorldExample: MD5 (128-bit) was broken in practice because its birthday attack bound is only 2^64 operations.

questions.prompt: What happened to the MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions in modern cybersecurity?
options: They suffered collision attacks in practice and were officially retired from security use
They were purchased by Google and made private
They were converted into block ciphers
They were upgraded to 1024 bits
questions.explanation: Researchers demonstrated practical SHA-1 collisions in 2017 (SHAttered) and MD5 collisions in 2004 (Flame malware), causing NIST to deprecate both.
wrongExplanations: Correct! MD5 and SHA-1 are cryptographically broken; use SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-3.
They remain open public algorithms.
Hash functions cannot become block ciphers.
Their digest lengths remain 128 and 160 bits.
questions.realWorldExample: Google and CWI Amsterdam produced the first real SHA-1 collision in two distinct PDF documents in 2017.

questions.prompt: How many bits are in a SHA-256 hash digest?
options: 256 bits (32 bytes / 64 hexadecimal characters)
128 bits
512 bits
64 bits
questions.explanation: SHA-256 outputs exactly 256 bits of digest, typically displayed as 64 hexadecimal characters.
wrongExplanations: Correct! 256 bits = 32 bytes = 64 hex characters.
128 bits is MD5.
512 bits is SHA-512.
64 bits is a tiny checksum.
questions.realWorldExample: Bitcoin block headers are hashed with double SHA-256 (SHA-256(SHA-256(Block))).

questions.prompt: What is the internal design structure used by SHA-256 to process blocks of data?
options: Merkle-Damgård construction with Davies-Meyer compression function
Feistel network
Vigenère table
Caesar dial
questions.explanation: SHA-256 splits padded messages into 512-bit chunks, feeding each into a Davies-Meyer compression function operating on eight 32-bit state words.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Merkle-Damgård construction processes sequential chunks through a compression function.
Feistel networks are used in block ciphers like DES.
Vigenère is a classical cipher.
Caesar is a 1-byte shift.
questions.realWorldExample: SHA-3 uses a fundamentally different 'sponge construction' (Keccak) to avoid length-extension attacks.

ashRecap: A cryptographic hash is a one-way digital fingerprint. Change even one single letter, and the entire fingerprint explodes into something completely new!
